text: TET-84: a verification that did not run says so

Every observation in this memo was taken against tetel at 74d4622d, the tip of main after PR #30, with no tracked file modified. The first two parts of TET-84 are merged. PR #28 made a verification that ran out of budget report `timeout` rather than `unavailable`, and PR #29 raised the default budget. This memo is the third part: what the author is told when a verification does not complete.
What this design delivers

Three changes to the `verify` object that every `fact`, `claim` and `prose` reply carries, and nothing outside it. The reply that delivers a failed verification says why, through the record's `detail`. Model or provider reply text is never included. Under the three failure statuses, `guidance` says the mint was not checked instead of describing findings that do not exist. A new `unverified` key names the mints whose latest verification failed, and it stays on every reply until each of them is re-verified. The tool description and docs/verify.md change with it.
The defect

A verification runs after its mint has replied, and its result arrives on some later reply: one record per call, oldest first. When it ends `timeout`, `unavailable` or `unparsable`, that later reply carries the status and nothing else about it. The record's `detail` stays in the log, because `block` only ever inserts a detail for `unauthorized`. The `guidance` beside it is the constant written for findings, which tells the author that a model found their text inconsistent with the evidence and asks them to read a quoted span that is not there. No reply after that one mentions the mint again. An author who misses one field on one reply has no way to learn that the mint was never checked. The run that opened TET-84 lost 19 of 61 mints this way.

text: Decision 1: the delivered record says why

The record already knows why it failed. `detail` is kept on every non-`ok` record, and on an `ok` whose literal, refuter or gate leg did not complete. The change is that the reply delivering such a record carries its `detail`. Most causes are fixed text, a status code, a transport error, a byte count or a budget, and those are exactly what an author needs to tell a slow provider from an exhausted key. Four of the twenty sources are different: they quote the model's or the provider's own reply. Those quotations stay in the log, for the reason the module already withholds an unverified quoted span. A reader shown text that looks like evidence will go and check it, and this text is not evidence.

The quotations are split off where they are written rather than trimmed from the finished string afterwards. Each of the four sites will write its explanation to `detail` and the quoted text to a separate field that only the log and `verify-report --spans` read. Trimming later would depend on the format of four strings that nothing else pins. The split also fixes a quiet fault in `verify-report`. The report groups identical `detail` strings, and a string ending in a per-reply excerpt is never identical to another, so today every such failure prints as its own line, mostly excerpt. The guarantee is per site, not structural: a fifth site could format reply text into `detail` and nothing in the type would stop it. The four tests below pin the four sites that exist.
Decision 2: guidance that matches the status

Under `timeout`, `unavailable` and `unparsable`, `guidance` becomes a second constant. It says the mint named by `for_mint` was not checked, that a missing `findings` means nothing was compared, and that `detail` says why. It also says what the author can do today. Repeating the same text starts no new verification, because the handlers skip a revision whose text and citations are unchanged, so only a real change re-checks the mint. `ok` keeps the existing constant, since it is the one status whose reply carries findings. The other statuses (`queued`, `skipped`, `off`, `gated`, `unauthorized`) are also misdescribed by the findings-shaped text, but none of them is a check that was attempted and lost. They are left alone and listed as a residual.
Documentation surface

The status vocabulary is stated in two places, and both change with the payload. The `claim` tool description gains one sentence: a delivered failure carries `detail` saying why, and `unverified` names the mints still unchecked. In docs/verify.md, "What comes back" stops tying `detail` to `unauthorized` alone, adds `unverified` to the keys that appear only when they have something to say, and notes that `guidance` differs under the three failure statuses.
Falsifying tests

Each test names the revert that turns it red. Two cover `detail` delivery: a planted `timeout`, and an `ok` with a failed refuter leg. Four cover the reply-text split, one per site, each driving a sentinel through a reply body and asserting that the sentinel is in the log field and absent from the reply. One covers `guidance` across the three failure statuses and `ok`. Four cover `unverified`. The first is a planted log that mixes a recovered mint, two failures, a withdrawn claim, and a mint whose later-started verification was appended first; that last case is the one that proves ordering by start rather than by log position. The others check the ten-id cap, absence when verification is disabled, and the two orders in which a legacy record without a start mark can meet a marked one.
Rejected alternatives

A key outside the `verify` object would separate "found nothing" from "did not look", which are exactly the two things an author must read together. Surfacing unverified mints in `check`, `brief` or the rendered memo would put a non-repeating model call inside the partitions that state what `check` covers. The module header rules that out for this reason. A retry or circuit breaker changes what the verifier does, and this design changes only what it says. A failure rate names no mint to act on and never falls when one is fixed. Refusing the mint would break the verifier's one hard rule: nothing in it can fail a mint.
Deferred and residual

Deferred: re-running a failed verification without changing the mint's text. After this change the author is told a mint is unchecked, but can clear it only by rewording it or changing its citations. A follow-up ticket should be filed if the list stays non-empty in practice. Residuals:
- The other five statuses keep the findings-shaped `guidance`.
- Keeping reply text out of `detail` is enforced per site by tests, not by the type.
- A mint minted while verification was off, or could not start, has no record and is never listed.
- A mint being re-verified stays listed under its old failure until the new record lands.
- A transport failure's `detail` carries the HTTP library's error text, which may name the endpoint but never the key.
Decision 3: the unchecked mints stay named

A status delivered once is easy to miss, so the failure has to persist until it no longer holds. `unverified` carries `count` and up to ten mint ids, and it rides on every reply that carries a `verify` object while verification is enabled, including replies on a verb that is not itself verified. A mint is on the list when its latest verification failed. "Latest" means highest revision, not last in the log. The log is in completion order, and a revision's verification can finish before the one it replaced. So `Subject` and `Record` gain the mint's revision count, which each verb's ledger already keeps, only increases, and cannot tie. Records written before the change have no revision and sort behind those that do. The tally comes from the log that `peek_delivered` already parses on every call, so it adds no read of verify.log. The claim ledger is read only when a failing mint is a claim, which is the one kind that can be withdrawn.

The record already knows why it failed. `detail` is kept on every non-`ok` record, and on an `ok` whose literal, refuter or gate leg did not complete, where it explains the `*_incomplete` qualifier. The change is that the reply delivering such a record carries its `detail`. Most causes are fixed text, a status code, a transport error, a byte count or a budget. A record can itself be `unauthorized`, from a typed leg with no endpoint. Its own detail then takes precedence over `missing`, which describes the configuration now rather than the one that failed. Four of the twenty sources are different: they quote the model's or the provider's own reply. Those quotations stay in the log, for the reason the module already withholds an unverified quoted span. A reader shown text that looks like evidence will go and check it, and this text is not evidence.

text: A verification runs after its mint has replied, and its result arrives on some later reply: one record per call, oldest first. Calls that overlap can each show the same record. When it ends `timeout`, `unavailable` or `unparsable`, the reply that delivers it carries the status and nothing else about it. The record's `detail` stays in the log, because `block` only ever inserts a detail for `unauthorized`. The `guidance` beside it is the constant written for findings, which tells the author that a model found their text inconsistent with the evidence and asks them to read a quoted span that is not there. Once the record has been delivered, no reply mentions the mint again. An author who misses one field has no way to learn that the mint was never checked.
